c:deadline_policy_t.why: not a QoS policy at all, despite the name. `nros_deadline_policy_t` (RELEASED / ACTIVATED / INHERITED) is RFC-0047's real-time SCHEDULING deadline interpretation -- a field of `nros_sched_context_t`, mirroring `nros_node::executor::sched_context::DeadlinePolicy`. The RTOS scenario is a periodic task whose deadline is measured from release, from activation, or inherited from its caller; rcl has no scheduling context so ROS 2 has nothing to compare it with. It appears in this stage because `topics.py`'s KEY_OVERRIDES maps `deadline_policy_t` to qos while its three siblings `sched_class_t`, `sched_priority_t` and `sched_context_t` map to exec -- the verdict is right, the shard is not.

c:executor_add_client_with_request_id.why: rclc ships a second registration entry point whose callback also receives the `rmw_request_id_t`. Ours has one registration verb: the correlation token is an `int64_t` sequence number that `nros_client_send_request` returns and `nros_service_send_response_raw` takes back (see the service stage's `cpp:Client::create_request_header`), and it belongs to the ENTITY, not to a second `add_*` overload. A registration entry point per callback shape is the `executor-owns-no-entity-storage` rule seen from the executor's side.

c:executor_add_on_shutdown_callback.why: The post-teardown half of `c:executor_add_pre_shutdown_callback`; rclc has neither. Runs after the session is closed, for what survives the middleware (release a GPIO, stop a peripheral clock). Issue 0790.

c:executor_add_pre_shutdown_callback.why: The ORDER is the feature: pre-shutdown callbacks run while the session is still open and every entity still works -- which is how a device publishes a final state, answers a last request, parks an actuator or releases a bus -- and on-shutdown callbacks run after the close. rclc has no shutdown hook of any kind -- rcl's `rcl_context_t` carries no callback list and rclc adds none -- so this has no ROS 2 C counterpart to correspond to; the C++ side does (`cpp:on_shutdown`). It exists because an RTOS node has nowhere else to release hardware: there is no OS to reclaim a claimed SPI or CAN peripheral, an armed DMA channel or an actuator holding its last commanded position. The platform constraint is no allocator: rclcpp's registration takes a `std::function<void()>` (a heap allocation per callback) and hands back a handle owning a `std::shared_ptr` to it. Ours is a fixed-capacity static table of `(extern "C" fn, void* context)` sized by `NROS_EXECUTOR_MAX_SHUTDOWN_CBS` (default 2, small on issue 0460's precedent that a per-entity static slot is a cost every image pays), and the handle is the SLOT INDEX with its phase packed in so it cannot remove the other phase's callback. rclcpp hangs these on `Context`; we have none (see `c:context_*` / `cpp:Context` in init.json), and the executor is what `shutdown` / `close` / `fini` is called on, so it owns the tables. Issue 0790.

c:executor_add_service_with_context.why: every nano-ros callback typedef already ends in `void *context`, and the pair is bound to the ENTITY at creation (RFC-0041/0043) rather than handed to the executor. So `nros_executor_add_service` IS rclc's with-context form -- rclc needs the variant only because its base callback has no context parameter. See `c:subscription_callback_t`.

c:executor_add_service_with_request_id.why: see `c:executor_add_client_with_request_id`; the deferred-reply path is `nros_service_take_request_raw` + `nros_service_send_response_raw(sequence_number, ...)`. (CORRECTED 2026-08-27, phase-379 W5: this named two symbols that do not work. `nros_service_send_response` was renamed from `nros_service_send_reply_raw` and is now a deprecated forwarder -- see `c:service_send_response_raw` in service.json. `nros_service_take_request` was, and still is, a permanent `NROS_RET_NOT_INIT` stub; its working twin was `nros_service_try_recv_request_raw`, renamed to `nros_service_take_request_raw` by phase-379 W6 decision 1; which of `take_request` / `take_request_raw` survives is `c:service_take_request`.) CORRECTED 2026-09-04 (phase-417): the sentence above described the CURRENT deferred-reply path using the retired `try_recv` spelling.

c:executor_bind_handle_to_sched_context.why: RFC-0002 section 4.2 / RFC-0047 / RFC-0079 -- the SchedContext surface, which ROS 2 has no counterpart for at all. A mixed-criticality image runs a 20 ms control loop and best-effort telemetry on ONE executor on ONE RTOS task, so the criticality ordering has to live in user space: N callbacks must not cost N kernel priority slots (RFC-0002 non-goal 3), and RFC-0079 exists because the raw kernel number is unwritable by hand -- each RTOS has its own range and its own DIRECTION. rclcpp's nearest answer is one `MultiThreadedExecutor` thread per priority, which an MCU cannot pay for. This is the primitive the group table is built on: bind one registered handle to one SchedContext, applied on the next spin cycle.

Registers one SchedContext (class + priority + period/budget/deadline) into the executor's fixed `NROS_EXECUTOR_MAX_SC` table; `NROS_RET_FULL` when it is exhausted.

c:executor_get_handle_count.why: how many arena slots are in use. The arena is a compile-time-sized table (`NROS_EXECUTOR_MAX_HANDLES`), so 'did my registrations fit?' is a real question with a cheap answer; rclc answers it only by failing the next `add_*`. See `c:executor_get_remaining_handles`.

c:executor_get_remaining_handles.why: the other half of `c:executor_get_handle_count`: remaining arena capacity, asked BEFORE registering. An image that registers entities conditionally at boot (a sensor that may or may not be present) needs to know whether the optional set still fits, rather than discovering it from a `NROS_RET_FULL` halfway through bring-up.

c:executor_get_zero_initialized.why: rcl's zero-init idiom under our naming; see `c:publisher_get_zero_initialized`.

c:executor_get_zero_initialized_executor.why: rclc's stuttering spelling -- the type name appears twice. Ours is `nros_executor_get_zero_initialized`, the method-style name on the type. See `c:get_zero_initialized_publisher`.

The enum VALUES (`NROS_EXECUTOR_ON_NEW_DATA` / `NROS_EXECUTOR_ALWAYS`) were not part of this row and did not move. c:executor_has_param.why: 'is this parameter declared?', asked without the six `rcl_interfaces/srv/*` servers being up. Parameters live on the EXECUTOR here rather than on a node (see the param stage's `c:executor_register_parameter_services`), and a device that bakes its parameter set (RFC-0045) wants a local existence check that costs no queryable slot -- `ZPICO_MAX_QUERYABLES` is 8 on embedded (issue 0460).

c:executor_is_valid.why: mirrors `rcl_context_is_valid` on the object that actually holds the session here; see `c:support_is_valid`. rclc ships no `rclc_executor_is_valid`.

c:executor_node_init.why: static entity storage plus one session: a node is created ON the executor (`nros_executor_node_init(executor, node, name, options)`) and lands in the executor's node table (`NROS_EXECUTOR_MAX_NODES`), so it cannot exist before one or be moved between two. rcl builds a node from an `rcl_context_t` and rclc adds it nowhere; see `cpp:Executor::add_node` for the same divergence in C++ and `cpp:Context` for why there is no separate context.

c:executor_ping.why: wire-level round trip -- is the XRCE agent / zenoh router still reachable, within `timeout_ms`. Mirrors micro-ROS's `rmw_uros_ping_agent`, which rclc has no counterpart for. The scenario is reconnect-on-link-loss: a device on a flaky radio has to distinguish 'nobody is publishing' from 'the session is dead' and re-open, and neither returns an error from `spin_some`.

c:executor_prepare.why: rclc pre-allocates its `rcl_wait_set` from the handles registered so far, so a later `spin` does not allocate. There is no wait set (rcl's wait set; the reason is stated in full at `cpp:WaitSet`.) and the arena is sized at compile time, so there is nothing to pre-allocate: static entity storage: the executor's entity table is an arena sized at compile time (`NROS_EXECUTOR_MAX_HANDLES`) with no allocator behind it, and a `HandleId` is an index into it. Registration is one-way -- no slot is ever reclaimed and no handle is ever invalidated.

c:executor_remove_*.why: rclc can drop a subscription, client, service, timer or guard condition from a spinning executor. static entity storage: the executor's entity table is an arena sized at compile time (`NROS_EXECUTOR_MAX_HANDLES`) with no allocator behind it, and a `HandleId` is an index into it. Registration is one-way -- no slot is ever reclaimed and no handle is ever invalidated. What a user loses: retiring an entity at runtime to reclaim its slot -- a mode change has to register every entity it may ever need at boot and gate them, which is also what a memory budget that must be known before flashing wants. This is a deliberate shape, not an oversight; if it is ever wanted, slot reuse needs handle generation counters first.

c:executor_remove_pre_shutdown_callback.why: Removal half of `c:executor_add_pre_shutdown_callback` -- rclcpp's `Context::remove_pre_shutdown_callback`, which the ROS 2 C API has no counterpart for. `NROS_RET_NOT_FOUND` rather than an error for an already-removed handle, and for a handle issued by the other phase. Issue 0790.

c:executor_state_t.why: an explicit executor lifecycle (uninitialised / initialised / spinning / shutdown) so a double-init or a use-after-fini is a returned code rather than undefined behaviour on a device that cannot report a crash. See `c:support_state_t`. Note the SPINNING state is the only place in the tree that models `rclcpp::Executor::is_spinning` -- and it is not exported; see `cpp:Executor::is_spinning`.

c:executor_stop.why: stop a spinning executor WITHOUT finalizing it -- flips `nros_executor_state_t` back from SPINNING to INITIALIZED so `nros_executor_spin`'s loop exits and the session stays open for a later spin. rclc's `rclc_executor_spin` has no way out at all. The scenario is a mode change on an RTOS task (safe-state, OTA staging) where tearing the middleware down and re-opening it costs a full discovery round. OUR LANGUAGES DISAGREE: this capability is spelled three ways and one language does not have it: C `nros_executor_stop`, Rust `Executor::halt` / `is_halted` / `halt_flag`, rclcpp `Executor::cancel` -- and C++ has NOTHING, because `Executor::spin` there exits only on `shutdown()`, which calls `nros_cpp_fini` and destroys the session. See `cpp:Executor::cancel`.

c:get_zero_initialized_guard_condition.why: rcl's free-function zero-init spelling; ours is `nros_guard_condition_get_zero_initialized`. See `c:get_zero_initialized_publisher`.

c:get_zero_initialized_wait_set.why: there is no wait-set type to zero-initialize. rcl's wait set; the reason is stated in full at `cpp:WaitSet`.

c:guard_condition_callback_t.why: the callback type belongs to the guard condition rather than to the executor's `add` call, because it is bound to the entity (RFC-0041). rcl's counterpart is the `rclc_gc_callback_t` passed to `rclc_executor_add_guard_condition` -- the `executor-owns-no-entity-storage` rule, seen as a type. See `c:subscription_callback_t`.

c:guard_condition_clear.why: clear the triggered flag; the other half of `c:guard_condition_is_triggered`, and absent from C++ and Rust for the same reason recorded there.

That is narrower than the `compile-time-options` signature rule this row used to cite, and it is the claim that is actually true. Seven ship and the correlator buckets all fourteen items `same` -- `nros_{node,publisher,subscription,service,client,action_client,action_server}_options_t` (`packages/api/nros-c/include/nros/nros_generated.h:1461,1729,2011,2474,2537,2556,2592`) plus a `*_get_default_options` for each, and `nros_node_options_t::domain_id_override` is a RUNTIME per-node domain. c:guard_condition_get_zero_initialized.why: rcl's zero-init idiom under our naming; see `c:publisher_get_zero_initialized`.

c:guard_condition_impl_t.why: rcl's pimpl; our handles carry their state inline. See `c:publisher_impl_t`.

c:guard_condition_init_from_rmw.why: adopts an already-constructed `rmw_guard_condition_t`. our RMW seam is the vtable (RFC-0035), not an entity accessor. See `c:node_get_rmw_handle`. There is no rmw-level object for a caller to hold, so there is nothing to adopt.

c:guard_condition_is_triggered.why: read the triggered flag without consuming it. The scenario is the RFC-0022 polling tier: a task that owns its own loop and never calls a callback still needs to see the flag an ISR set. rcl has no reader -- a wait set is the only way to observe an rcl guard condition. OUR LANGUAGES DISAGREE: C ships `is_triggered` + `clear`, C++ ships neither (only `trigger` and `is_valid`), and Rust's `GuardCondition` ships only `trigger`. A polling C++ or Rust user cannot do what a polling C user can.

c:guard_condition_set_callback.why: RFC-0041/0043 bind a callback to the ENTITY, and in C the binding is a SEPARATE call after `nros_guard_condition_init` -- which is exactly the after-the-fact installation shape we decline in C++ at `cpp:GuardCondition::set_on_trigger_callback`. OUR LANGUAGES DISAGREE: the guard condition is created three different ways, from three different owners, with three different callback bindings: C `nros_guard_condition_init(guard, SUPPORT)` then `nros_guard_condition_set_callback(...)`; C++ `NODE.create_guard_condition(out, cb, ctx)`, one call, callback at creation; Rust `EXECUTOR.register_guard_condition(closure)` returning `(HandleId, GuardCondition)`. rclcpp constructs one free-standing from a `Context`. Nothing about no_std picks between these -- W5 has to pick one.

c:guard_condition_trigger.why: the ours-only half of `c:trigger_guard_condition`; recorded so the pair is visible from both sides. Thread-safe and lock-free -- it stores into an atomic flag in the executor's arena and then fires the runtime wake hook, so an ISR or a foreign task can release a `spin_once` already blocked in `drive_io`.

c:shutdown_callback_t.why: `void (*)(void* context)` -- the shutdown-hook signature. A LOCAL typedef in nros-c rather than a re-export of `nros_node::ShutdownCallbackFn`, because cbindgen runs with `parse_deps = false` and a foreign type in an `extern "C"` signature degrades to an opaque struct C cannot call through. rclc has no shutdown hook, so no counterpart. Issue 0790.

c:trigger_guard_condition.why: RE-VERDICTED 2026-08-26 (phase-379 W5), was `rename`. rcl's free-function spelling `rcl_trigger_guard_condition(rcl_guard_condition_t *)`; ours is `nros_guard_condition_trigger` (`packages/api/nros-c/include/nros/nros_generated.h:4618`). The WORD already matches -- only the ORDER differs, and that order is our C API's single convention, `nros_<entity>_<verb>`. So the old row's 'the spelling is ours to align' was never a statement about one symbol: the identical clause sits on `c:publish` and `c:send_response`, and honouring it inverts the convention across the whole C surface. The class already has a settled precedent in the other direction -- `c:get_zero_initialized_guard_condition` and `c:get_zero_initialized_publisher` are both `declined` for exactly this reason. What a user loses: rcl's verb-first spelling; a ported rcl node rewrites `rcl_trigger_guard_condition(&gc)` as `nros_guard_condition_trigger(&gc)`. Ours half: `c:guard_condition_trigger`.

rename.resolution: re-verdicted `declined` -- same class as the zero-init family, which is already declined; nros_<entity>_<verb> is the C convention and rcl's verb-first ORDER is what we decline, the word itself already matches

c:wait.why: `rcl_wait` -- the blocking call at the centre of the protocol. rcl's wait set; the reason is stated in full at `cpp:WaitSet`. Ours is `nros_executor_spin_some(executor, timeout_ns)`, which drives I/O through the RMW vtable and dispatches every ready arena entry in one pass.

c:wait_set_*.why: rcl's wait set; the reason is stated in full at `cpp:WaitSet`.

c:wake_state_t.why: caller-declared storage for one wake callback's `(fn, ctx)` pair, passed into `nros_*_set_wake_callback` and kept alive at the same address while the entity is polling. It exists because there is no allocator to put a closure in: the caller declares the slot next to the entity. See the pubsub stage's `c:subscription_set_wake_callback` for the capability itself.

cpp:AnyExecutable.why: An rclcpp internal, not user API -- it is the wait-set result type its executors pass between themselves. A user writes neither the type nor its fields. RFC-0002's executor is not built from it.

cpp:CallbackGroup::CallbackGroup.why: ours is `CallbackGroup(const char* name)`, theirs is `CallbackGroup(CallbackGroupType, bool automatically_add_to_executor_with_node)` -- two arguments each and nothing in common, which is why the correlator calls it arity-only. rclcpp's `CallbackGroupType` is a CONCURRENCY policy -- `MutuallyExclusive` or `Reentrant` -- and it only means anything to a multi-threaded executor deciding whether two callbacks from one group may run at once. RFC-0002 puts one executor on one RTOS task with non-preemptive run-to-completion dispatch, so every group is mutually exclusive by construction and `Reentrant` is unrepresentable: there is no second thread to be reentrant from. The axis our group carries instead is a NAME that `system.toml` maps to a scheduling tier (RFC-0047, RFC-0079) -- the thing a mixed-criticality image actually needs from grouping. `automatically_add_to_executor_with_node` (rclcpp's second constructor argument) is meaningless for the same reason as `cpp:Executor::add_node`.

cpp:CallbackGroup::automatically_add_to_.why: the flag that decides whether an executor picks this group up when its node is added. Nodes are created BY the executor here and are never added to one; see `cpp:Executor::add_node`.

rust:Executor::*age_table.why: the same for `now - header.stamp` age monitors (RFC-0052 W3b.2) -- 'this pose is stale' is a different question from 'this publisher missed its deadline'. See `rust:Executor::*monitor_table`.

rust:Executor::*component*.why: the component enrolment table the `nros::node!` macro expands into -- how many slots exist, which are filled, and each enrolled component's state. Machinery a generated entry point needs and a hand-written user does not; issue 0784. RFC-0043/0044.

rust:Executor::*dispatch*.why: the generated-entry-point dispatch table: reserve a slot, count them, and invoke one by index. A static table indexed by slot is how a callback reaches its component body with no trait object and no allocation. Machinery `nros::node!` expands into; issue 0784.

rust:Executor::*domain_id.why: read and set the ROS domain after open. rclrs takes it from the environment through the context (`Context::default_from_env`); an image has no environment, so the domain arrives over RFC-0045's baked ladder and stays settable for the boot path that resolves it. See `c:get_default_domain_id`.

rust:Executor::*monitor_table.why: installs and reads the RFC-0052 contract-monitor table -- per-entity rate and deadline expectations, baked by codegen into a `&'static [MonitorSpec]`. It is a table rather than a registration call because it must be a compile-time constant in flash on a target with no allocator. rclcpp's nearest is per-entity QoS deadline events; this is the whole system's contract in one place, which is what an on-target safety monitor needs.

rust:Executor::*sched*.why: RFC-0002 section 4.2 / RFC-0047 / RFC-0079 -- the SchedContext surface, which ROS 2 has no counterpart for at all. A mixed-criticality image runs a 20 ms control loop and best-effort telemetry on ONE executor on ONE RTOS task, so the criticality ordering has to live in user space: N callbacks must not cost N kernel priority slots (RFC-0002 non-goal 3), and RFC-0079 exists because the raw kernel number is unwritable by hand -- each RTOS has its own range and its own DIRECTION. rclcpp's nearest answer is one `MultiThreadedExecutor` thread per priority, which an MCU cannot pay for. The Rust face of the same surface the C API exposes: `create_sched_context`, `default_sched_context_id`, `sched_context`, `set_default_sched_context`, and the three binding forms -- `bind_handle_to_sched_context` (one callback), `bind_group_sched` (RFC-0047's group name) and `bind_node_name_sched` (phase-272's degenerate per-node case).

rust:Executor::*violation*.why: drain the contract violations the monitors recorded (`drain_violations`), count the ones dropped when the fixed buffer overflowed (`violations_dropped`), and gate reporting (`set_report_violations`). The bounded buffer plus an explicit dropped count is the no-allocator shape: a device cannot grow a violation log, and silently losing entries would make the monitor lie. rclcpp raises QoS events through callbacks instead.

rust:Executor::add_on_shutdown_callback.why: The post-teardown half of `rust:Executor::add_pre_shutdown_callback`; rclrs has neither. Issue 0790.

rust:Executor::add_pre_shutdown_callback.why: The ORDER is the feature: pre-shutdown callbacks run while the session is still open and every entity still works -- which is how a device publishes a final state, answers a last request, parks an actuator or releases a bus -- and on-shutdown callbacks run after the close. rclrs has no shutdown hook at all -- no `Context` callback list, no free function -- so there is nothing on the rclrs side to correspond to. It exists because an RTOS node has nowhere else to release hardware while its entities still work. The platform constraint is no allocator: rclcpp's registration takes a `std::function<void()>` (a heap allocation per callback) and hands back a handle owning a `std::shared_ptr` to it. Ours is a fixed-capacity static table of `(extern "C" fn, void* context)` sized by `NROS_EXECUTOR_MAX_SHUTDOWN_CBS` (default 2, small on issue 0460's precedent that a per-entity static slot is a cost every image pays), and the handle is the SLOT INDEX with its phase packed in so it cannot remove the other phase's callback. rclcpp hangs these on `Context`; we have none (see `c:context_*` / `cpp:Context` in init.json), and the executor is what `shutdown` / `close` / `fini` is called on, so it owns the tables. Issue 0790.

rust:Executor::arena_capacity.why: how many arena bytes an executor was GIVEN and how many its registered entities actually claimed. No upstream analogue because upstream has no arena: rclcpp allocates each entity on the heap, so "how much of the pre-sized block is in use" is not a question it can ask. Here `ARENA_SIZE` is derived by budgeting EVERY slot at the ActionClient worst case, and the arena is a BUMP allocator held INLINE in the `Executor` value -- on the task stack, where `mem-report` cannot see it. So the allocator has always known the exact claimed total and had no way to say it: a timer-only executor claims 32 bytes of 74,240. These two accessors are how an image, a test, or the boot advisory finds the number to put in `NROS_EXECUTOR_ARENA_SIZE`. Issue 0900.

rust:Executor::close.why: release the session and the arena without dropping the value, so a caller holding an executor in a `static` can tear the middleware down and report the result. `Drop` cannot return an error, and an embedded slot is never deallocated.

rust:Executor::create_node.why: ours is `create_node(&mut self, name: &str) -> NodeHandle`, rclrs's is `create_node(&self, options) -> Arc<Node>`. Two differences, both structural: ours takes `&mut self` because the node is allocated in the executor's arena (static entity storage: the executor's entity table is an arena sized at compile time (`NROS_EXECUTOR_MAX_HANDLES`) with no allocator behind it, and a `HandleId` is an index into it. Registration is one-way -- no slot is ever reclaimed and no handle is ever invalidated.), and it hands back a borrowing `NodeHandle` rather than an `Arc` -- no allocator, and RFC-0043/0044 make the Rust API a declarative component model where a user implements the `Node` trait rather than holding one. See `cpp:Executor::create_node`.

rust:Executor::create_node_on*.why: create a node bound to a NAMED RMW backend (and optionally its own domain) on an executor that opened several. The scenario is the bridge image RFC-0002's shared executor makes possible: one RTOS task, one arena, two transports, a node on each. rclrs has one middleware per context.

rust:Executor::declare_remap.why: installs one `from -> to` name remap in the executor's fixed remap table. rclrs remaps through `__ns:=` / `topic:=` arguments on the command line, which no image has (RFC-0045); launch resolves the mapping and it is baked or declared here instead. See `cpp:remove_ros_arguments`.

rust:Executor::epoch_now_us.why: wall-clock microseconds since the UNIX epoch, or `None` when the target has no epoch source. RFC-0052: `header.stamp` is ROS (wall) time while the executor's own accounting is monotonic, so age monitoring needs both clocks and has to be able to say that one is absent -- a baked `max_age_ms` with no epoch source is a BAKE-time error, never a silently dead monitor. rclcpp assumes an OS clock.

rust:Executor::from_session*.why: builds an executor around a session someone else opened -- the C API's entry point (`nros_support_init` opens the session, then `nros_executor_init` wraps it) and the board/BSP paths. It exists because the C and C++ surfaces are implemented ON this type, and their lifecycle splits session creation from executor creation the way rcl does. rclrs has no counterpart: an rclrs executor never adopts a foreign handle. See `rust:Executor::open*`.

rust:Executor::group_active.why: the predicate behind `rust:Executor::set_active_groups`, public so generated tier entry points can skip declaring an entity that this tier will never dispatch.

rust:Executor::halt*.why: request the spin loop to stop and hand out the shared halt flag for a signal handler or another task. rclrs's counterpart is `ExecutorCommands::halt_spinning`, reached through the async command channel this stage declines (see `rust:Executor::commands`); ours is an `AtomicBool` plus a wake, so it works from an ISR with no allocation. OUR LANGUAGES DISAGREE: C spells it `nros_executor_stop`, Rust `halt`, and C++ cannot do it at all -- see `cpp:Executor::cancel`.

rust:Executor::is_halted.why: reads the flag `rust:Executor::halt*` sets -- the only 'is this executor still supposed to be spinning?' predicate in any of our three languages, and it is phrased inversely to rclcpp's. See `cpp:Executor::is_spinning`.

rust:Executor::node*.why: the executor's node TABLE -- `nodes`, `node`, `node_mut`, `node_id_by_name`, `node_session_mut`, `node_builder`. static entity storage: the executor's entity table is an arena sized at compile time (`NROS_EXECUTOR_MAX_HANDLES`) with no allocator behind it, and a `HandleId` is an index into it. Registration is one-way -- no slot is ever reclaimed and no handle is ever invalidated. A node is a record in a fixed table addressed by `NodeId`, not an `Arc<Node>` a caller keeps, so reaching one means asking the executor. RFC-0043/0044: the Rust API is a declarative component model. See `rust:Executor::create_node` and `cpp:Executor::node_builder`.

rust:Executor::open*.why: the executor OWNS the session here, so construction is `Executor::open(&ExecutorConfig)` rather than rclrs's `Context::create_executor` (see `rust:Context::create_executor` and `cpp:Context`). The variants are all constraint-shaped, not taste: `open_sized` takes an explicit `ExecutorSizing` because the arena is compile-time sized; the `*_in` suffix takes CALLER-provided backing storage (no allocator -- an image places the arena in a static, not on a heap); `open_multi` opens several RMW sessions on one executor because a gateway image bridges two transports from one RTOS task (RFC-0002); `open_with_rmw` pins the backend by registry name when more than one is linked in (issue 0687); `open_threaded` spawns the spin loop as a platform task and returns a `ThreadHandle`.

rust:Executor::params*.why: the executor-owned parameter store. Parameters live on the EXECUTOR here rather than on a node, because the six `rcl_interfaces/srv/*` servers are registered once per image against `ZPICO_MAX_QUERYABLES` = 8 (issue 0460), not once per node. See the param stage and `c:executor_has_param`.

rust:Executor::register_guard_condition.why: creates the guard condition ON THE EXECUTOR and returns `(HandleId, GuardCondition)`. rclrs constructs a `GuardCondition` from a `Context` and adds it to a wait set; rclrs's wait-set machinery; the reason is stated in full at `cpp:WaitSet`. so the executor has to own the flag -- it lives in the arena, which is what makes the handle `Send + Sync` with no allocation. See `c:guard_condition_set_callback` for the three different owners our three languages create this from.

rust:Executor::resolve_entity_name*.why: applies the remap table plus the node namespace to a source name and hands back the resolved topic/service. It is public because generated entry points and the C surface both resolve names through this one path rather than each concatenating strings. See `rust:Executor::declare_remap`.

rust:Executor::session*.why: accessors onto the session the executor owns (`session`, `session_mut`, `session_handle`, `session_ptr`) plus its I/O health (`session_io_healthy`, `session_io_failures`). The pointer forms exist because the C/C++ surfaces are built on this type and need the raw handle across the FFI boundary; see `cpp:Executor::handle`. The health counters are the RTOS half: a device on a flaky link has to distinguish 'no traffic' from 'transport is failing' without an exception to catch (RFC-0018). rclrs exposes no session at all.

rust:Executor::set_active_groups.why: restricts dispatch to a named set of callback groups. RFC-0047 maps a group to a tier and an orchestrated image runs ONE executor per tier task, so each task's executor has to dispatch only its own tier's callbacks out of a shared registration set. rclcpp achieves the same by adding different groups to different executors, which needs an executor object per tier and a heap to hold them.

rust:Executor::set_fault_handler.why: one process-wide `fn(&Violation)` called when a contract monitor fires -- the hook an image parks an actuator or trips a watchdog from. It is a bare `fn` pointer, not a closure, because there is no allocator to box one. See `rust:Executor::*violation*` and `cpp:on_shutdown` for the shutdown-side gap.

rust:Executor::set_invocation.why: switches one registered callback between ON_NEW_DATA and ALWAYS at runtime -- rclc's invocation mode, which rclrs has no counterpart for. See `c:executor_handle_invocation_t`.

rust:Executor::set_min_stack_headroom_by.why:
declares the minimum stack headroom the executor's own thread must keep, in bytes; `0` (the default) disables the `stack-headroom-runtime` rule. The companion to `rust:Executor::*monitor_table` for a resource ROS 2 never has to watch: a hosted node's stack grows, an RTOS task's does not, and an overflow there corrupts a NEIGHBOUR's state rather than faulting cleanly.

Set by the ENTRY rather than inferred, because the entry is the only party that knows what stack it handed over -- the executor never sees `stack_bytes` and no portable query returns a task's total stack, so neither an absolute floor nor a percentage can be computed here. Same "ask, do not assume" as issue 0667's `stack_bytes` floors.

Newly VISIBLE to this report on 2026-09-05, not newly written: `nros_platform_api::task` was gated on `alloc` because it also holds the allocating spawn helper, so the rule's own platform query (`stack_unused_bytes`, a bare `extern` that allocates nothing) did not compile in a no-alloc image and the surface was never extracted. phase-425 moved the gate onto `PlatformTask` alone. rclcpp has no counterpart -- a desktop thread's stack grows on demand and the OS reports the overrun; an RTOS task's does not, and the overrun is silent memory corruption. Same family as `rust:Executor::*violation*`.

rust:Executor::set_node_identity.why: sets node name and namespace after open, because RFC-0046 makes LAUNCH the authority on node identity and an image is told its name at boot rather than parsing argv (there is none). rclrs fixes identity at `create_node`. See `c:support_init_named`.

rust:Executor::set_primary_identity.why: the same for the RMW name and locator; see `rust:Executor::set_node_identity`.

rust:Executor::set_semantics.why: selects interleaved versus Logical Execution Time dispatch; see `rust:ExecutorSemantics`, including the note that C++ cannot do this.

rust:Executor::set_trigger.why: installs the trigger predicate that decides whether a cycle's ready set is dispatched at all -- rclc's `rclc_executor_set_trigger` (`ANY` / `ALL` / `ONE` / a user function), which rclrs has no counterpart for. A time-triggered image dispatches only when EVERY input of a frame has arrived, which is the difference between a deterministic control cycle and a partially-updated one.

rust:Executor::shutdown_callback_count.why: How many hooks are registered for a phase. The tables are FIXED-capacity (`NROS_EXECUTOR_MAX_SHUTDOWN_CBS`, default 2), so "did my registration land, and how much room is left" is a question only a bounded table raises; rclcpp's nearest thing, `Context::get_pre_shutdown_callbacks`, hands back the heap-allocated callbacks themselves. Issue 0790.

rust:Executor::spin_async.why: rclrs drives spin_async on an async runtime (async-std/tokio). no_std targets have neither, and RFC-0002 puts one executor per RTOS task rather than a task-stealing runtime. The blocking `spin` is the whole model here.

rust:Executor::wake*.why: release a `spin_once` blocked in the backend's `drive_io` before its poll timeout expires, from another task or an ISR, and hand out the handle that does it. rust:Executor::release_jitter.why: Landed 2026-09-04 (`55324cc33`, sched). Ours-only, and there is no upstream name to align to: neither the recorded rclrs nor rclcpp surface contains `jitter` or `late_wake` at all. Here `spin_period` IS the release, so lateness is measurable and is the figure of merit a periodic RTOS task is judged by. RFC-0052's real-time observability: `(max_release_jitter_us, late_wakes, total_wakes)` for a `spin_period` loop. rclcpp has no counterpart because it does not own the release -- a periodic rclcpp node is a wall timer on a general-purpose executor, and the lateness a scheduler introduces is not a quantity rclcpp is in a position to measure. Ours is, because one executor owns one RTOS task (RFC-0002) and the period is the task's own.

The RATIO is the point, not the maximum alone: one late wake in ten thousand is a glitch, ten thousand in ten thousand means the period cannot be met -- two different failures that a single max cannot tell apart. Zero on a clockless build, where `spin_period` refuses to run at all (issue 0709), so there is nothing to have measured.

rust:Executor::clear_release_jitter_stat.why: phase-417 W-M2 note: see `rust:Executor::release_jitter`. The reset half -- a measurement window is only meaningful if a caller can start one, and without this the counters are since-boot forever. rclcpp has no counterpart for the same reason it has none for the reading.
